subject: Religionskunskap 1
title: Religion in conflicts and global contexts
sourceSummary: How religion can function as a marker of identity in conflicts without being the root cause, examples of religiously motivated peace work, freedom of religion as a human right, and religion's connection to migration.

questions.prompt: Which statement gives the most nuanced, religious-studies-sound description of religion's role in armed conflicts?
questions.opener: Consider the difference between a conflict being about religion and religion being used as a marker of identity or group belonging in a conflict that is also driven by other factors.
choices: All armed conflicts in the world are caused solely by religion
Religion is never involved in armed conflicts in any way

Religion often functions as a marker of identity that separates groups in a conflict, but conflicts are usually simultaneously driven by factors such as power, resources, politics and history — pointing to religion alone as the cause is an oversimplification
Conflicts involving religious groups are always solely about theological disagreements
questions.explanation: Research in religious studies and conflict studies shows that religion often functions as a marker of identity that makes groups distinguishable in a conflict, but that conflicts in practice are usually driven by a combination of factors: power, control over resources, politics, historical injustices and group identity, with religion being one of several components rather than the sole cause. Simplifying a conflict to being "about religion" risks concealing these other, often decisive, driving forces.

questions.prompt: What is more specifically meant by religion functioning as a "marker of identity" in a conflict?
questions.opener: Consider how religious affiliation is sometimes used to distinguish "us" from "them", even when the conflict is really about something else.
choices: That religion is the only factor that caused the conflict from the start

That religious affiliation is used to mark boundaries between groups and strengthen group cohesion, which can reinforce a conflict that already has other underlying causes, such as political power or resources
That religious symbols are entirely without significance in a conflict situation
That all parties to a conflict always share the same religion
questions.explanation: Religion functioning as a marker of identity means that religious affiliation is used to draw boundaries between "us" and "the others" and strengthen cohesion within one's own group, which can reinforce and deepen a conflict whose underlying causes often lie in, for example, political power, land or resources. Religion then becomes part of how the conflict is expressed and organised, rather than necessarily its original cause.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is an example of religiously motivated peace work?
questions.opener: Think of people or organisations who have drawn their commitment to peace and justice from their religious conviction.
choices: A religious leader who calls for armed conflict against another group

Religious organisations and leaders who, based on their faith, work for reconciliation, dialogue between groups and conflict resolution, for example through interfaith peace initiatives or mediation in areas affected by conflict
Abstaining entirely from engaging in social issues
Only one religion in world history having ever carried out peace work
questions.explanation: Religiously motivated peace work means that individuals or organisations, based on their religious conviction about, for example, compassion and justice, actively work for reconciliation, dialogue and conflict resolution — this occurs within most religious traditions, for instance through interfaith peace initiatives or religiously motivated mediation in conflict areas. Calling for armed conflict is the opposite of peace work.

questions.prompt: How is freedom of religion defined as a human right, for example according to the UN's Universal Declaration of Human Rights?
questions.opener: Consider that the right covers more than just the freedom to believe in a god.
choices: The right of the state to force all citizens into the same religion
The right of every person to freely choose, practise, change or abstain from a religion or belief, both individually and together with others
The right to practise a religion only in secret, never publicly
A right that only applies within certain countries and is not internationally recognised
questions.explanation: Freedom of religion as a human right, recognised among other places in the UN's Universal Declaration of Human Rights (Article 18), means the right of every person to freely adopt, practise, change or abstain from a religion or belief, both privately and publicly, individually and in community with others. The right therefore also protects the right not to believe, and to openly practise one's faith together with others.

questions.prompt: What is an example of a violation of freedom of religion, from a human rights perspective?
questions.opener: Consider the difference between criticising a religion in public debate and banning or punishing people for their faith.
choices: A journalist writing a critical opinion piece about a religious representative's statement
A state banning a religious minority from building its places of worship, or punishing citizens for changing religion
A person choosing on their own to leave their religion
Different religious communities existing side by side in the same country
questions.explanation: A state banning a religious minority from erecting places of worship, or punishing citizens for changing or leaving a religion, are examples of violations of freedom of religion as a human right. Critical debate about religious statements, as well as an individual's own free choices in matters of faith, fall instead within the scope of freedom of expression and freedom of religion respectively.

questions.prompt: In what way can religion be relevant to study in connection with migration?
questions.opener: Consider religion's role both as a cause of fleeing and as a support in a new country.
choices: Religion never has any connection to migration

Religion can, on the one hand, be one of several reasons people are forced to flee, for example through persecution because of faith, and, on the other, function as a source of community, identity and support for migrants in a new country
Migrants always belong to exactly the same religion as the majority population in the country they flee to
Only a single religion in the world has ever been linked to migration
questions.explanation: Religion can be relevant to migration in several ways: persecution because of religious affiliation is in some cases a direct cause of flight, while at the same time religious communities, for example a congregation or mosque in the new country, often become an important source of social support, community and preserved identity for people fleeing or migrating. Migrants naturally belong to a wide range of different religions and worldviews, not a single shared one.

questions.prompt: A news headline describes a conflict as a "religious war". Explain, using religious studies concepts, why such a headline can be misleading, and what a more nuanced analysis might look like.
questions.opener: Distinguish between religion as a marker of identity and religion as a root cause, and consider what other factors often play a part in conflicts.
questions.answer: Calling a conflict a "religious war" suggests that religious doctrine or theological disagreement is in itself the main or sole cause of the conflict. A more nuanced, religious-studies analysis instead distinguishes between religion as a marker of identity, that is, how religious affiliation is used to separate "us" and "the others" and strengthen group cohesion, and the underlying, often more decisive driving forces behind the conflict, which can involve control over land and resources, political power, historical injustices or ethnic identity. In many conflicts described as "religious", religious affiliation coincides with other social dividing lines, such as ethnicity or region, which makes religion a clear and visible marker, while the actual causes of the fighting may lie on another level entirely. A nuanced analysis would therefore examine the conflict's history, economic and political interests, and how religious identity is interwoven with these factors, rather than stopping at a simplified headline.
steps: Identify what the headline "religious war" suggests: that religion itself is the main cause of the conflict.
Introduce the concept of a marker of identity: religion can distinguish groups without being the root cause of the conflict.
List other common underlying factors in conflicts: power, resources, politics, historical injustices, ethnicity.
Explain how religious affiliation often coincides with other social dividing lines, which makes religion visible without it being the whole explanation.
Propose a more nuanced analysis that weighs together several factors, rather than reducing the conflict to a single cause.

questions.prompt: Summarise religion and conflict, religious peace work, freedom of religion, and religion and migration.
questions.opener: Go through conflict, peace work, freedom of religion and migration in turn.
questions.answer: Religion and conflict: religion often functions as a marker of identity that separates groups, but conflicts are usually driven by several interacting factors such as power, resources, politics and history — religion is rarely the sole cause. Religious peace work: religious leaders and organisations work, based on their faith, for reconciliation, dialogue and conflict resolution, e.g. through interfaith initiatives. Freedom of religion: a human right (among others the UN's Article 18) to freely adopt, practise, change or abstain from a religion or belief, individually or in community, privately or publicly · violated for example through bans on places of worship or punishment for changing faith. Religion and migration: religious persecution can be a cause of flight, while religious community often becomes a source of support and identity for migrants in a new country.
